aristotle-four-causes: Aristotle's doctrine of the four causes holds that a full explanation of anything requires answering four distinct questions about it: what it is made of (the material cause), what form or structure makes it the kind of thing it is (the formal cause), what brought it into being (the efficient cause), and what end or purpose it serves (the final cause). He developed this scheme in the Physics and Metaphysics as a response to earlier thinkers who, he argued, had grasped only fragments of true explanation. Because it treats purpose as a genuine kind of cause, the theory undergirds Aristotle's broadly teleological view of nature.
aristotle-soul: In his treatise On the Soul (De Anima), Aristotle defines the soul not as a separate substance lodged in the body but as its form: the organizing principle that makes a living thing the living thing it is. On this view the soul is the actuality of a body that has life potentially within it, so that soul and body are related as shape is to matter rather than as two independent items. He distinguishes nutritive, perceptive, and rational capacities, arguing that living things possess these powers in ascending degrees, with reason the distinctive mark of the human soul.
aristotle-friendship: Aristotle devotes two books of the Nicomachean Ethics to philia, the bond of affection and goodwill that he counts among the goods essential to a flourishing life. He distinguishes three kinds: friendships of utility and of pleasure, which last only as long as the advantage or enjoyment does, and friendships of virtue, in which each person wishes the other well for the other's own sake. This last, complete form is rare and enduring, and for Aristotle it is both a school of good character and one of life's greatest goods.
aristotle-potentiality: Aristotle draws a fundamental distinction between potentiality (dynamis) and actuality (energeia or entelecheia) to explain how change and being are possible. A thing is potentially what it can become and actually what it presently is: an acorn is potentially an oak, and becoming an oak is the actualization of that potential. Introduced largely in the Metaphysics, the pair lets Aristotle answer earlier puzzles about whether anything can genuinely come to be, and it grounds his account of motion, growth, and the priority of the actual over the merely possible.
political-animal: In the Politics Aristotle famously describes the human being as by nature a political animal (zoon politikon), meaning that we are constituted to live in an organized community and can fully realize our nature only within one. Unlike other social creatures, humans possess speech and reason, which enable them to deliberate about justice and the common good and so to form a city (polis). On this view the state is not an artificial contract imposed on naturally solitary individuals but the natural setting in which human flourishing becomes possible.
aristotle-practical-wisdom: Phronesis, usually rendered as practical wisdom or prudence, is for Aristotle the intellectual virtue that governs good action in particular circumstances. Unlike theoretical knowledge, which concerns unchanging truths, practical wisdom is the capacity to perceive what the situation requires and to deliberate well about how to achieve worthwhile ends. In the Nicomachean Ethics it is the master virtue of conduct, since without it the moral virtues lack direction, and it cannot be reduced to rules but is acquired through experience and habituation.
heraclitean-flux: Heraclitus of Ephesus, writing around 500 BCE, is remembered for the doctrine that everything is in ceaseless change, captured in the saying that one cannot step into the same river twice. Beneath this flux, however, he posited the logos, a unifying rational principle or measure that orders the world's constant transformations and holds opposites in tension. His view that reality is a dynamic balance of strife and change stands as an early counterpoint to those who sought a stable, unchanging foundation for things.
parmenidean-being: Parmenides of Elea, active in the early fifth century BCE, argued through a rigorous chain of reasoning that whatever truly is must be one, eternal, indivisible, and changeless, since to speak of what is not is to speak of nothing at all. From this he concluded that change, plurality, and coming-to-be are illusions of the senses, and that reason alone reveals genuine reality. His radical denial of change set the terms for much later Greek metaphysics, forcing successors to reconcile the evidence of the senses with the demands of logic.
zeno-paradoxes: Zeno of Elea, a disciple of Parmenides in the fifth century BCE, devised a series of paradoxes intended to defend his teacher's claim that motion and plurality are illusory. The best known, such as Achilles and the tortoise and the arrow that seems never to move, argue that motion leads to contradictions when space and time are treated as infinitely divisible. Whether or not they succeed, the paradoxes pose deep puzzles about infinity, continuity, and the structure of space and time that have occupied philosophers and mathematicians ever since.
atomism: Ancient atomism, developed by Leucippus and especially Democritus in the fifth century BCE, holds that reality consists of countless indivisible particles, atoms, moving through empty space, or void. All apparent qualities and changes are explained by the arrangement, motion, and combination of these unchanging bodies, so that nothing exists but atoms and the void. This thoroughly materialist and mechanistic picture offered an early way to reconcile the reality of change with a stable underlying substance, and it profoundly influenced later thinkers such as Epicurus.
pythagorean-harmony: The harmony of the spheres is a doctrine associated with Pythagoras and his followers in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, who held that number and proportion are the ultimate principles of reality. Struck by the discovery that musical intervals correspond to simple numerical ratios, they extended this insight to the cosmos, imagining that the heavenly bodies move according to harmonious mathematical relationships and even produce an inaudible music. The idea expresses the deeper Pythagorean conviction that the order of the universe is fundamentally mathematical.
sophist-relativism: The dictum that man is the measure of all things comes from the sophist Protagoras, active in fifth-century BCE Athens, and expresses a relativist view of truth and value. On this reading things are as they appear to each perceiver, so that what is true, good, or just is relative to individuals or communities rather than fixed by any absolute standard. The position challenged the notion of objective knowledge and provoked lasting responses from Plato and others, who saw in it a threat to the possibility of genuine truth.
cynicism: Cynicism was an ancient Greek philosophical movement, epitomized by Diogenes of Sinope in the fourth century BCE, that urged living in accordance with nature and in defiance of social convention. The Cynics held that virtue is the only good and that happiness comes from freedom, self-sufficiency, and the rejection of wealth, status, and artificial desires, which they regarded as sources of servitude. Diogenes dramatized these ideas through a deliberately austere and provocative way of life, making the movement as much a practice as a set of doctrines.
ship-of-theseus: The Ship of Theseus is a puzzle about identity over time, reported by the biographer Plutarch, who noted that the Athenians preserved Theseus's ship by gradually replacing its decaying planks. This raises the question of whether the ship remains the same object once every original part has been swapped out, and whether identity resides in matter, form, or continuity. The thought experiment has become a standard way of probing what makes something persist as one and the same thing despite the replacement of its parts.
epicurean-pleasure: Epicurus, founding his school in Athens around 300 BCE, taught that pleasure is the highest good and the natural aim of life, but he understood pleasure primarily as the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance rather than as sensual indulgence. This tranquil state, ataraxia, is best achieved through modest desires, friendship, and freedom from the fears of death and the gods, which he sought to dispel with his atomist physics. Epicurean ethics thus prizes a serene and self-sufficient contentment over intense or fleeting gratifications.
